studies.title: Neural coding of distinct statistical properties of reward information in humans.
studies.abstract: Brain processing of reward information is essential for complex functions such as learning and motivation. Recent primate electrophysiological studies using concepts from information, economic and learning theories indicate that the midbrain may code two statistical parameters of reward information: a transient reward error prediction signal that varies linearly with reward probability and a sustained signal that varies highly non-linearly with reward probability and that is highest with maximal reward uncertainty (reward probability = 0.5). Here, using event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging, we disentangled these two signals in humans using a novel paradigm that systematically varied monetary reward probability, magnitude and expected reward value. The midbrain was activated both transiently with the error prediction signal and in a sustained fashion with reward uncertainty. Moreover, distinct activity dynamics were observed in post-synaptic midbrain projection sites: the prefrontal cortex responded to the transient error prediction signal while the ventral striatum covaried with the sustained reward uncertainty signal. These data suggest that the prefrontal cortex may generate the reward prediction while the ventral striatum may be involved in motivational processes that are useful when an organism needs to obtain more information about its environment. Our results indicate that distinct functional brain networks code different aspects of the statistical properties of reward information in humans.

studies.title: Hierarchical and Nonlinear Dynamics in Prefrontal Cortex Regulate the Precision of Perceptual Beliefs.
studies.abstract: Actions are shaped not only by the content of our percepts but also by our confidence in them. To study the cortical representation of perceptual precision in decision making, we acquired functional imaging data whilst participants performed two vibrotactile forced-choice discrimination tasks: a fast-slow judgment, and a same-different judgment. The first task requires a comparison of the perceived vibrotactile frequencies to decide which one is faster. However, the second task requires that the estimated difference between those frequencies is weighed against the precision of each percept-if both stimuli are very precisely perceived, then any slight difference is more likely to be identified than if the percepts are uncertain. We additionally presented either pure sinusoidal or temporally degraded "noisy" stimuli, whose frequency/period differed slightly from cycle to cycle. In this way, we were able to manipulate the perceptual precision. We report a constellation of cortical regions in the rostral prefrontal cortex (PFC), dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) and superior frontal gyrus (SFG) associated with the perception of stimulus difference, the presence of stimulus noise and the interaction between these factors. Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) of these data suggested a nonlinear, hierarchical model, whereby activity in the rostral PFC (evoked by the presence of stimulus noise) mutually interacts with activity in the DLPFC (evoked by stimulus differences). This model of effective connectivity outperformed competing models with serial and parallel interactions, hence providing a unique insight into the hierarchical architecture underlying the representation and appraisal of perceptual belief and precision in the PFC.

studies.title: Functional development of fronto-striato-parietal networks associated with time perception.
studies.abstract: Compared to our understanding of the functional maturation of executive functions, little is known about the neurofunctional development of perceptive functions. Time perception develops during late adolescence, underpinning many functions including motor and verbal processing, as well as late maturing higher order cognitive skills such as forward planning and future-related decision making. Nothing, however, is known about the neurofunctional changes associated with time perception from childhood to adulthood. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging we explored the effects of age on the brain activation and functional connectivity of 32 male participants from 10 to 53 years of age during a time discrimination task that required the discrimination of temporal intervals of seconds differing by several hundred milliseconds. Increasing development was associated with progressive activation increases within left lateralized dorsolateral and inferior fronto-parieto-striato-thalamic brain regions. Furthermore, despite comparable task performance, adults showed increased functional connectivity between inferior/dorsolateral interhemispheric fronto-frontal activation as well as between inferior fronto-parietal regions compared with adolescents. Activation in caudate, specifically, was associated with both increasing age and better temporal discrimination. Progressive decreases in activation with age were observed in ventromedial prefrontal cortex, limbic regions, and cerebellum. The findings demonstrate age-dependent developmentally dissociated neural networks for time discrimination. With increasing age there is progressive recruitment of later maturing left hemispheric and lateralized fronto-parieto-striato-thalamic networks, known to mediate time discrimination in adults, while earlier developing brain regions such as ventromedial prefrontal cortex, limbic and paralimbic areas, and cerebellum subserve fine-temporal processing functions in children and adolescents.

studies.title: Dissociation in decision bias mechanism between probabilistic information and previous decision.
studies.abstract: Target detection performance is known to be influenced by events in the previous trials. It has not been clear, however, whether this bias effect is due to the previous sensory stimulus, motor response, or decision. Also it remains open whether or not the previous trial effect emerges via the same mechanism as the effect of knowledge about the target probability. In the present study, we asked normal human subjects to make a decision about the presence or absence of a visual target. We presented a pre-cue indicating the target probability before the stimulus, and also a decision-response mapping cue after the stimulus so as to tease apart the effect of decision from that of motor response. We found that the target detection performance was significantly affected by the probability cue in the current trial and also by the decision in the previous trial. While the information about the target probability modulated the decision criteria, the previous decision modulated the sensitivity to target-relevant sensory signals (d-prime). Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we also found that activation in the left intraparietal sulcus (IPS) was decreased when the probability cue indicated a high probability of the target. By contrast, activation in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) was increased when the subjects made a target-present decision in the previous trial, but this change was observed specifically when the target was present in the current trial. Activation in these regions was associated with individual-difference in the decision computation parameters. We argue that the previous decision biases the target detection performance by modulating the processing of target-selective information, and this mechanism is distinct from modulation of decision criteria due to expectation of a target.

studies.title: Global motion perception deficits in autism are reflected as early as primary visual cortex.
studies.abstract: Individuals with autism are often characterized as 'seeing the trees, but not the forest'-attuned to individual details in the visual world at the expense of the global percept they compose. Here, we tested the extent to which global processing deficits in autism reflect impairments in (i) primary visual processing; or (ii) decision-formation, using an archetypal example of global perception, coherent motion perception. In an event-related functional MRI experiment, 43 intelligence quotient and age-matched male participants (21 with autism, age range 15-27 years) performed a series of coherent motion perception judgements in which the amount of local motion signals available to be integrated into a global percept was varied by controlling stimulus viewing duration (0.2 or 0.6 s) and the proportion of dots moving in the correct direction (coherence: 4%, 15%, 30%, 50%, or 75%). Both typical participants and those with autism evidenced the same basic pattern of accuracy in judging the direction of motion, with performance decreasing with reduced coherence and shorter viewing durations. Critically, these effects were exaggerated in autism: despite equal performance at the long duration, performance was more strongly reduced by shortening viewing duration in autism (P < 0.015) and decreasing stimulus coherence (P < 0.008). To assess the neural correlates of these effects we focused on the responses of primary visual cortex and the middle temporal area, critical in the early visual processing of motion signals, as well as a region in the intraparietal sulcus thought to be involved in perceptual decision-making. The behavioural results were mirrored in both primary visual cortex and the middle temporal area, with a greater reduction in response at short, compared with long, viewing durations in autism compared with controls (both P < 0.018). In contrast, there was no difference between the groups in the intraparietal sulcus (P > 0.574). These findings suggest that reduced global motion perception in autism is driven by an atypical response early in visual processing and may reflect a fundamental perturbation in neural circuitry.

studies.title: The Effect of Wealth Shocks on Loss Aversion: Behavior and Neural Correlates.
studies.abstract: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) first demonstrated that when individuals decide whether or not to accept a gamble, potential losses receive more weight than possible gains in the decision. This phenomenon is referred to as loss aversion. We investigated how loss aversion in risky financial decisions is influenced by sudden changes to wealth, employing both behavioral and neurobiological measures. We implemented an fMRI experimental paradigm, based on that employed by Tom et al. (2007). There are two treatments, called RANDOM and CONTINGENT. In RANDOM, the baseline setting, the changes to wealth, referred to as wealth shocks in economics, are independent of the actual choices participants make. Under CONTINGENT, we induce the belief that the changes in income are a consequence of subjects' own decisions. The magnitudes and sequence of the shocks to wealth are identical between the CONTINGENT and RANDOM treatments. We investigated whether more loss aversion existed in one treatment than another. The behavioral results showed significantly greater loss aversion in CONTINGENT compared to RANDOM after a negative wealth shock. No differences were observed in the response to positive shocks. The fMRI results revealed a neural loss aversion network, comprising the bilateral striatum, amygdala and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex that was common to the CONTINGENT and RANDOM tasks. However, the ventral prefrontal cortex, primary somatosensory cortex and superior occipital cortex, showed greater activation in response to a negative change in wealth due to individual's own decisions than when the change was exogenous. These results indicate that striatum activation correlates with loss aversion independently of the source of the shock, and that the ventral prefrontal cortex (vPFC) codes the experimental manipulation of agency in one's actions influencing loss aversion.

studies.title: Gain control explains the effect of distraction in human perceptual, cognitive, and economic decision making.
studies.abstract: When making decisions, humans are often distracted by irrelevant information. Distraction has a different impact on perceptual, cognitive, and value-guided choices, giving rise to well-described behavioral phenomena such as the tilt illusion, conflict adaptation, or economic decoy effects. However, a single, unified model that can account for all these phenomena has yet to emerge. Here, we offer one such account, based on adaptive gain control, and additionally show that it successfully predicts a range of counterintuitive new behavioral phenomena on variants of a classic cognitive paradigm, the Eriksen flanker task. We also report that blood oxygen level-dependent signals in a dorsal network prominently including the anterior cingulate cortex index a gain-modulated decision variable predicted by the model. This work unifies the study of distraction across perceptual, cognitive, and economic domains.

studies.title: Putamen Activation Represents an Intrinsic Positive Prediction Error Signal for Visual Search in Repeated Configurations.
studies.abstract: We investigated fMRI responses to visual search targets appearing at locations that were predicted by the search context. Based on previous work in visual category learning we expected an intrinsic reward prediction error signal in the putamen whenever the target appeared at a location that was predicted with some degree of uncertainty. Comparing target appearance at locations predicted with 50% probability to either locations predicted with 100% probability or unpredicted locations, increased activation was observed in left posterior putamen and adjacent left posterior insula. Thus, our hypothesis of an intrinsic prediction error-like signal was confirmed. This extends the observation of intrinsic prediction error-like signals, driven by intrinsic rather than extrinsic reward, to memory-driven visual search.

studies.title: Hierarchical prediction errors in midbrain and basal forebrain during sensory learning.
studies.abstract: In Bayesian brain theories, hierarchically related prediction errors (PEs) play a central role for predicting sensory inputs and inferring their underlying causes, e.g., the probabilistic structure of the environment and its volatility. Notably, PEs at different hierarchical levels may be encoded by different neuromodulatory transmitters. Here, we tested this possibility in computational fMRI studies of audio-visual learning. Using a hierarchical Bayesian model, we found that low-level PEs about visual stimulus outcome were reflected by widespread activity in visual and supramodal areas but also in the midbrain. In contrast, high-level PEs about stimulus probabilities were encoded by the basal forebrain. These findings were replicated in two groups of healthy volunteers. While our fMRI measures do not reveal the exact neuron types activated in midbrain and basal forebrain, they suggest a dichotomy between neuromodulatory systems, linking dopamine to low-level PEs about stimulus outcome and acetylcholine to more abstract PEs about stimulus probabilities.

studies.title: Vasopressin increases human risky cooperative behavior.
studies.abstract: The history of humankind is an epic of cooperation, which is ubiquitous across societies and increasing in scale. Much human cooperation occurs where it is risky to cooperate for mutual benefit because successful cooperation depends on a sufficient level of cooperation by others. Here we show that arginine vasopressin (AVP), a neuropeptide that mediates complex mammalian social behaviors such as pair bonding, social recognition and aggression causally increases humans' willingness to engage in risky, mutually beneficial cooperation. In two double-blind experiments, male participants received either AVP or placebo intranasally and made decisions with financial consequences in the "Stag hunt" cooperation game. AVP increases humans' willingness to cooperate. That increase is not due to an increase in the general willingness to bear risks or to altruistically help others. Using functional brain imaging, we show that, when subjects make the risky Stag choice, AVP down-regulates the BOLD signal in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), a risk-integration region, and increases the left dlPFC functional connectivity with the ventral pallidum, an AVP receptor-rich region previously associated with AVP-mediated social reward processing in mammals. These findings show a previously unidentified causal role for AVP in social approach behavior in humans, as established by animal research.

studies.title: Effects of Prior Knowledge on Decisions Made Under Perceptual vs. Categorical Uncertainty.
studies.abstract: Humans use prior knowledge to bias decisions made under uncertainty. In this fMRI study we predicted that different brain dynamics play a role when prior knowledge is added to decisions made under perceptual vs. categorical uncertainty. Subjects decided whether shapes belonged to Category S - smoother - or Category B - bumpier - under both uncertainty conditions, with or without prior knowledge cues. When present, the prior knowledge cue, 80/20 or 50/50, indicated that 80 and 20% (or 50 and 50%) were the chances that responding "S" and "B" (or vice versa) would be correct. During perceptual uncertainty, shapes were degraded with noise. During categorical uncertainty, shapes were ambiguous. Adding the 80/20 cue increased activation during perceptual uncertainty in bilateral lateral occipital (LO) cortex and left middle frontal gyrus (MidFG), and decreased activity in bilateral LO cortex during categorical uncertainty. Right MidFG and other frontoparietal regions were active in all conditions. The results demonstrate that left MidFG shows activation changes, suggestive of an influence on visual cortex, that depend on the factor that makes the decisions difficult. When sensory evidence is difficult to perceive, prior knowledge increases visual cortical activity. When the sensory evidence is easy to perceive but difficult to interpret, prior knowledge decreases visual cortical activity.

studies.title: Discriminating grotesque from typical faces: evidence from the Thatcher illusion.
studies.abstract: The discrimination of thatcherized faces from typical faces was explored in two simultaneous alternative forced choice tasks. Reaction times (RTs) and errors were measured in a behavioural task. Brain activation was measured in an equivalent fMRI task. In both tasks, participants were tested with upright and inverted faces. Participants were also tested on churches in the behavioural task. The behavioural task confirmed the face specificity of the illusion (by comparing inversion effects for faces against churches) but also demonstrated that the discrimination was primarily, although not exclusively, driven by attending to eyes. The fMRI task showed that, relative to inverted faces, upright grotesque faces are discriminated via activation of a network of emotion/social evaluation processing areas. On the other hand, discrimination of inverted thatcherized faces was associated with increased activation of brain areas that are typically involved in perceptual processing of faces.

studies.title: Neural correlates of speeded as compared with delayed responses in a stop signal task: an indirect analog of risk taking and association with an anxiety trait.
studies.abstract: The stop signal task (SST) is widely used to explore neural processes involved in cognitive control. By randomly intermixing stop and go trials and imposing on participants to respond quickly to the go but not the stop signal, the SST also introduces an indirect element of risk, which participants may avert by slowing down or ignore by responding "as usual," during go trials. This "risk-taking" component of the SST has to our knowledge never been investigated. The current study took advantage of variability of go trial reaction time (RT) and compared the post-go go trials that showed a decrease in RT (risk-taking decision) and those post-go go trials that showed an increase in RT ("risk-aversive" decision) in 33 healthy individuals who underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging during the SST. This contrast revealed robust activation in bilateral visual cortices as well as left inferior parietal and posterior cingulate cortices, amygdala, and middle frontal gyrus (P < 0.05, family-wise error [FWE] corrected). Furthermore, we observed that the magnitude of amygdala activity is positively correlated with trait anxiety of the participants. These results thus delineated, for the first time, a neural analog of risk taking during stop signal performance, highlighting a novel aspect and broadening the utility of this behavioral paradigm.

studies.title: Positive interaction of social comparison and personal responsibility for outcomes.
studies.abstract: We formulate and test a model that allows sharp separation between two different ways in which environment affects evaluation of outcomes, by comparing social vs. private and personal responsibility vs. chance. In the experiment, subjects chose between two lotteries, one low-risk and one high-risk. They could then observe the outcomes. By varying the environment between private (they could observe the outcome of the chosen lottery and the outcome of the lottery they had not chosen) and social (they could observe the outcome of the lottery chosen by another subject) we can differentiate the response and brain activity following the feedback in social and private settings. The evidence suggests that envy and pride are significant motives driving decisions and outcomes evaluation, stronger than private emotions like regret and rejoice, with ventral striatum playing a key role. When we focus on the outcome evaluation stage we demonstrate that BOLD signal in ventral striatum is increasing in the difference between obtained and counterfactual payoffs. For a given difference in payoffs, striatal responses are more pronounced in social than in private environment. Moreover, a positive interaction (complementarity) between social comparison and personal responsibility is reflected in the pattern of activity in the ventral striatum. At decision stage we observe getting ahead of the Joneses effect in ventral striatum with subjective value of risk larger in social than in private environment.

Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (original empirical data), I2 (fMRI during risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making), I3 (relevant human sample performing such tasks).

fulltext_screening_results.reason: This fMRI study (Daw et al., 2011) reports whole-brain group fMRI results during a two-stage sequential reinforcement-learning task. Inclusion criteria met: I4 (fMRI during a decision-making task), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise maps reported), I7 (acceptable participant group—healthy adults), and I8 (results reported in text/figures). However, the study does not report any qualifying risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making contrast as required (e.g., risky>safe; high-uncertainty>low-uncertainty; hard>easy). Its analyses focus on reward prediction errors and model-based vs model-free valuation rather than contrasts of risk/ambiguity/perceptual difficulty (I5 not met). Thus it is excluded under E5 (task is not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual DM contrast of the types required). Full text appears complete.

This fMRI study of slot-machine outcomes reports whole-brain, group-level activation maps with coordinates and includes pathological and non-pathological gambler groups (meets I6, I7, I8). However, it does not test risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making contrasts as defined by the review (e.g., risky>safe, high- vs low-risk, ambiguity contrasts). The reported contrasts are outcome-processing contrasts (wins vs losses, large-win vs small-win), not condition contrasts that manipulate decision uncertainty or risk at the time of choice. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E5 (task is not a risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making task per meta-analysis definitions). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (task mapped to risky/ambiguous/perceptual DM) and I5 (required decision-making contrasts). Full text appears complete. Hence EXCLUDED.

This fMRI study tested human participants performing a risky decision-making gambling task (GIG task) during scanning, manipulating risk via risky vs safe options and quota conditions. The fMRI analyses report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts comparing decision conditions (quota-severity contrast and Low/High > Non/Imp and Non/Imp > Low/High), with activation maps and coordinates and cluster correction. Participants were healthy humans. Thus the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI risky decision-making, condition-vs-condition contrasts, group whole-brain results, participant eligibility, and availability of results in text/figures. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, only ROI, only connectivity without activation, contrasts vs rest only) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an fMRI study in human participants using a perceptual decision-making task (random dot kinematograms) with manipulations of stimulus coherence and reward. The paper reports within-task parametric contrasts of coherence (e.g., effects of low vs. high coherence/unsigned coherence and signed coherence) and epoch comparisons, and performs group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SnPM permutation testing) in addition to ROI analyses. Participants were healthy adults. Results and whole-brain statistical maps/clusters are described and displayed. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not only baseline contrasts, includes whole-brain results). Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8.

This study reports an fMRI experiment with healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (gender-ambiguous face perception) and compares ambiguous vs. unambiguous conditions, so it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5 and I7. However, the fMRI analysis is performed as ROI-based variance analyses (bilateral SPL and IPL) without reporting a group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E6 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results) and fails to satisfy inclusion criterion I6 (whole-brain, voxelwise group task map not provided). Full text appears complete. Based on these points, the study is excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a two-alternative forced-choice task about ambiguous (morphed) facial expressions (perceptual/ambiguous decision-making). The paper reports within-task contrasts relevant to decision-making ("sad" versus "happy" choices for ambiguous faces, and 100% sad versus 100% happy) and investigates task-evoked, group-level whole-brain voxelwise activity using SPM with coordinates and cluster statistics. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I4 (fMRI during ambiguous/perceptual DM), I5 (within-task contrasts comparing decision conditions), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise maps reported), I7 (eligible participant group: healthy adults), and I8 (whole-brain results reported as coordinates/tables). No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not only ROI or connectivity, not task>rest only, not non-empirical). Full text appears complete.

This is an fMRI study in humans that administered a perceptual decision-making task (mental rotation) during scanning and reports within-task contrasts (e.g., 80° vs 0° rotation; hard > easy). Group-level whole-brain voxelwise activation maps are reported and described (corrected for multiple comparisons), and ROI results complement those maps. Participant groups (Pre-HD and healthy controls) are acceptable. The paper therefore meets the review’s requirements for a perceptual decision-making fMRI study with condition-vs-condition contrasts and whole-brain results. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion), so inclusion is supported.

This fMRI study used the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), a canonical risky decision-making task, with event-related parametric modulators indexing trial-by-trial risk/reward (e.g., Inflate*p(Explode), Success*p(Explode)). Analyses were performed at the group level using whole-brain voxelwise statistics (SPM5) and report whole-brain clusters/tables linking task contrasts to behavior and substance use outcomes. The study therefore provides within-task condition contrasts (parametric high-risk vs low-risk modulation), whole-brain task activation maps, and involves a clinical human sample; results are reported in tables/figures and described in the text. The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present in the provided content. On this basis the study satisfies inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and violates no exclusion criteria. It is appropriate to include in the meta-analysis of risky decision-making fMRI studies.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it used fMRI while participants performed a risky decision-making task (Risky-Gains), and reports a direct risky > safe contrast (risky vs. safe choices). Analyses are whole-brain, voxelwise group-level maps (paired t-tests, voxel-wise correlations) with reported coordinates and figures, satisfying whole-brain evidence and acceptable reporting. Participant group (adolescents with excess weight) is eligible. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not only ROI/connectivity, not task>rest only). Full text appears complete (intro, methods, results, discussion). Therefore it should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

Although the study used fMRI in humans performing a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task (I4), reported group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (I6), included healthy participants (I7), and presented whole-brain results in text/figures (I8), it does not report a decision-making contrast that matches the meta-analysis inclusion forms (e.g., risky>safe, high-risk>low-risk, ambiguity>non-ambiguity, hard>easy). The primary reported contrasts are reward vs neutral, loss vs neutral, and parametric prediction-error regressors rather than the required risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision contrasts (I5 not met). No exclusion criteria from E3–E9 are triggered. Therefore excluded for failing to meet I5.

(a) Exclusion IDs met: none. (b) Inclusion IDs met: I4 (fMRI was conducted while participants performed a risky gamble task interleaved with the social PD), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported), I7 (healthy participants were tested), I8 (whole-brain results are reported in tables/figures). (c) Inclusion IDs not met: I5 — the paper does not report a qualifying decision-making contrast of the form required for the meta-analysis (e.g., risky > safe, high-risk > low-risk, risk > certainty, or an explicit risky decision > control-task contrast). The gamble task analyses model outcome (e.g., $0, $1, $2) and use outcome-based contrasts and a task-by-payoff interaction ((CD-CC)-($0-$2)), rather than a direct risky-versus-safe or decision-phase contrast. Therefore it does not provide the required decision-making condition contrast for inclusion. Full text appears complete, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This is an fMRI study in which human participants performed a categorization task that includes ambiguous decision trials (inverse base rate effect). The paper reports within-task contrasts (e.g., comparisons of activation on ambiguous trials depending on response type and model-based parametric modulators for similarity vs. dissimilarity evidence) and presents group-level, whole-brain voxelwise statistical maps (cluster-corrected) with tables and figures. Participants are healthy adults and full methods, results, and discussion are present. No exclusion criteria are met (no PET, no ROI-only, not task>rest only). Thus the study meets inclusion criteria for ambiguous decision-making fMRI (I4), contains relevant within-task contrasts (I5), reports group whole-brain maps (I6), involves an eligible participant group (I7), and reports whole-brain results in text/figures/tables consistent with acceptable reporting (I8).

This is an fMRI study in human participants performing an ecologically valid risky decision-making task (virtual sexual ‘hook up’ game) during scanning (meets I4). It reports condition-vs-condition contrasts including SRD > Conversational (an active control) and SRD > implicit baseline (meets I5). Group-level voxelwise/statistical maps and TFCE cluster results with peak coordinates are reported for task contrasts and between-group comparisons (reported clusters/coordinates and whole-brain covariate analyses), satisfying whole-brain, group-level reporting (I6) and coordinate reporting (I8). Participant sample (MSM, including meth users and non-users) is an acceptable participant group (I7). No exclusion criteria are met: contrasts are not only against implicit baseline (E3 not met), not PET (E4), task is risky decision-making (E5 not met), whole-brain results/coordinates are reported (E6 not met), and this is empirical fMRI activation (E7, E8 not met). Therefore I include this study for the meta-analysis. Full text appears complete for screening.

This full text reports an fMRI study in human participants performing a perceptual decision-making (categorization) task manipulating motion coherence (perceptual salience) and distance from a category boundary (categorical salience). The paper reports condition-vs-condition analyses including parametric contrasts (e.g., BOLD modulation with motion coherence: low coherence > high coherence) and ANOVA interactions, with whole-brain, group-level voxelwise maps (cluster-corrected) and ROI confirmation. Participants are healthy adults. The manuscript includes complete sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore it satisfies I4 (fMRI during perceptual DM), I5 (condition/parametric contrasts comparing decision conditions), I6 (whole-brain group voxelwise maps), I7 (eligible participant group), and I8 (whole-brain results clearly described). No exclusion criteria apply (no PET, no task>rest-only contrasts, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not non-empirical). Full text appears complete.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a decision-making task manipulating rule certainty vs uncertainty. It reports within-task contrasts (uncertain > certain and certain > uncertain) that map onto ambiguous decision-making (high uncertainty > low uncertainty). Group-level whole-brain voxelwise GLM results are reported (FEAT, cluster-thresholded maps, figures, and tabulated cluster descriptions), and whole-brain ROI/network analyses are also provided. Full article includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study involves human participants performing a decision-making task that includes risk (probabilities) and effort, and reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results. However, the neuroimaging contrasts reported focus on Shannon entropy (behavioral inconsistency), subjective value in low-entropy pairs, and secured-effort contrasts (NRNE>NRME). The paper does not present a contrast that matches the meta-analysis’ required risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision contrasts (e.g., risky > safe, high-risk > low-risk, ambiguity > non-ambiguity, or hard > easy). Importantly, the task is a combined effort-and-risk paradigm and much of the reported imaging results center on effort-related and inconsistency-related contrasts; the meta-analysis explicitly excludes effort-based choice studies (E5). Therefore, although I4, I6, I7 and I8 are satisfied (fMRI during risky/effort decisions, whole-brain maps, eligible participant group, and clear reporting), the study is excluded because it violates E5 and does not provide the requisite risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision contrast (I5 not met).

This fMRI study used a probabilistic reversal learning task that involves decision making under uncertainty (probabilistic reward contingencies and reversals), matching the review's focus on risky/ambiguous decision-making. fMRI was recorded while participants performed the task (I4). The authors report within-task model-derived contrasts (reward prediction error as a parametric modulator at feedback) and group-level comparisons (including main effects of RPE and OCD>control contrasts), satisfying the requirement for at least one decision-making contrast (I5) and providing whole-brain, group-level voxelwise statistical maps (cluster-corrected) suitable for meta-analysis (I6). Participant groups (patients and healthy controls) are acceptable (I7). Results are reported in-text and in supplementary figures/tables (I8). The study does not violate exclusion criteria: it is not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and includes within-group task effects rather than only between-group contrasts. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study is excluded because its decision-making task is economic social bargaining (iterated Ultimatum Game), not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (Exclusion E5). Inclusion criteria met: I5 (it contains decision > control contrasts such as UG > CTRL), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses were performed), and I8 (whole-brain results and coordinates are reported). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (the task is social/reciprocity-focused rather than risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). The full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present), so exclusion is based on task domain mismatch with the review objective rather than missing information.

This is an fMRI study in humans using the Iowa Gambling Task (a risky/ambiguous decision-making paradigm) with an explicit active control task. The paper reports within-group and group-level, whole-brain voxelwise activation maps (IGT > control) with statistical thresholds and cluster reporting, and provides coordinate/figure-based whole-brain results. Participants include patient and healthy control groups; methods, results, and discussion are complete in the provided full text. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.

This fMRI study collected whole-brain, group-level task-evoked data while human participants performed a probabilistic reward-guided decision-making task with uncertain/anti-correlated reward contingencies and reversals. The task involves decision-making under probabilistic uncertainty (risk/ambiguity) and includes within-task condition contrasts (reward vs. punishment; positive vs. negative prediction error parametric modulators) and PE-related contrasts used in whole-brain analyses. Results are reported as voxelwise group-level maps with coordinates and FWE correction. Participant groups (alcohol-dependent patients and healthy controls) are acceptable. The full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 are satisfied; no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a limited-offer decision task that manipulates risk/uncertainty (accept vs wait with chance of losing the offer). The authors report group-level, voxelwise SPM analyses (whole-brain and ROI), including parametric contrasts for choice conflict (entropy/high vs low) and expected precision (state-dependent confidence), with reported whole-brain significant clusters and midbrain ROI peaks. These constitute within-task condition comparisons (e.g., high vs low conflict/precision) relevant to risky/uncertain decision-making. The manuscript contains full methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets I4 (fMRI during risky/uncertain decision-making), I5 (within-task contrasts comparing decision conditions via parametric modulators), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise maps reported), I7 (human participant sample acceptable), and I8 (results reported as coordinates/figures). No exclusion criteria apply (not PET; not only baseline contrasts; not ROI-only; not connectivity-only; empirical data). Full text appears complete.

This study tests decision-making during fMRI with economic games involving risk/ambiguity (assurance and chicken games) and reports fMRI contrasts (e.g., AG vs CG). However, the paper’s neuroimaging results are reported only as region-of-interest (ROI) analyses because their exploratory whole-brain analysis yielded no significant voxels ("No voxels survived FWE correction") and no whole-brain coordinate/map results are provided for the task contrasts. Therefore the study does not provide a usable group-level, whole-brain task-evoked statistical map as required. Inclusion met: I4 (fMRI during risky/ambiguous decision tasks), I5 (between-condition contrast AG vs CG), I7 (healthy human participants). Inclusion not met: I6 (no reported whole-brain group-level/voxelwise task activation map). Exclusion applied: E6 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results). Full text appears complete.

This fMRI study used a probabilistic reversal learning task with monetary rewards and punishments, which constitutes decision-making under uncertainty (risky/ambiguous DM). The experiment collected whole-brain task-evoked fMRI data during the task and reports whole-brain one-sample and between-group voxelwise analyses (FWE-corrected), including contrasts separating punished and rewarded trials and correlations with computational model parameters. These meet the meta-analysis requirements for (I4) fMRI during a risky/ambiguous decision-making task, (I5) within-task condition contrasts (punished vs rewarded and parametric modulators), (I6) whole-brain group-level voxelwise maps reported, (I7) allowed participant groups (adolescent patients and healthy controls), and (I8) clear reporting of whole-brain results in text/figures/tables. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not baseline-only contrasts, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and includes within-group task effects). Full text appears complete with methods, results, and discussion.

Full text is complete. Inclusion criteria met: I4 (fMRI during a probabilistic/uncertainty feedback task that involves anticipation of gains/losses), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses reported), I7 (participant groups acceptable), I8 (whole-brain results reported in tables/figures). Inclusion criterion not met: I5 — the study does not report any qualifying decision-making contrast of the forms required (e.g., risky > safe, high-uncertainty > low-uncertainty, hard > easy). The main reported contrasts are valence-based (gain vs loss anticipation; gain vs loss outcomes) rather than risk/ambiguity or perceptual difficulty contrasts (no bivalent > non-bivalent or analogous ambiguity contrasts are reported). No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) apply. Therefore the study is excluded because it fails to meet I5 (required contrast specification) despite meeting other inclusion criteria.

This fMRI study used a probabilistic reversal learning (PRL) decision-making task with monetary feedback and modeled three feedback conditions (win, lose-stay, lose-shift) at first level and a whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analysis at second level. The authors report whole-brain group results for the lose-shift condition (FWE-corrected maps, clusters) and gPPI connectivity as supplementary analysis. The task involves uncertainty/probabilistic feedback (decision-making under uncertainty) and provides within-task condition contrasts (feedback conditions) qualifying under the review definitions. Participant groups are acceptable and results are reported as whole-brain statistical maps in the text/figures/SI. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, connectivity-only, baseline-only contrasts) apply. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so is complete.

This study reports task fMRI in human participants performing a risky multi-step gambling decision-making task (Goal-Instructed Gambling task). It includes within-task condition contrasts that directly compare decision states (quota-severity and strategy-optimization contrasts, e.g., Imp>High>Low>Easy and Low/High>Non/Imp), and reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses with cluster-size correction and peak coordinates (dlPFC, dACC, AI, dmPFC). Results include within-task contrasts and ROI/correlation follow-ups, and the full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not only baseline contrasts, not ROI-only, not only connectivity, and not non-empirical). Full text appears complete.

This study reports task-based fMRI in human participants performing a 6-armed bandit decision-making task (explore vs exploit), providing within-task contrasts (explore > exploit and exploit > explore) that map onto high-uncertainty vs low-uncertainty decision-making (ambiguous DM). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) analyses with tables/figures and cluster correction. Participants are an eligible sample (smokers), and the full article contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, connectivity-only, task>rest-only, or only between-group contrasts) are violated. Thus the study meets the review’s inclusion requirements for fMRI studies of decision-making under uncertainty and provides usable whole-brain contrasts for meta-analysis.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in which human participants performed a sequential risk-taking task (deciding whether to open more boxes with a hidden loss), satisfying the requirement for a risky decision-making task. The paper includes within-task contrasts (e.g., Opt vs Nopt, Nopt vs Devil, GF vs MF) comparing decision-related conditions rather than only task>baseline contrasts. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported with coordinate tables and FWE correction, satisfying the whole-brain evidence requirement; ROI analyses are present but are complemented by whole-brain results. Participants are healthy adults. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not only ROI, not resting-state/connectivity-only, not task>baseline only). Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusions apply.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in which healthy human participants performed a perceptual decision-making task (detecting degraded fearful vs neutral faces) while BOLD data were acquired. The paper presents condition-versus-condition contrasts (e.g., fear-cue vs neutral-cue; fearful-face vs neutral-face; FC/FF vs NC/FF) rather than task>baseline contrasts, and conducts group-level voxelwise SPM analyses (paired t-tests and mixed-model ANOVA) with reported whole-brain results and ROI-corrected results. Thus it provides whole-brain, group-level task-evoked activation maps from a perceptual decision-making paradigm. All relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This study includes an fMRI experiment (Experiment 1) in which human participants performed decision-making tasks that include a classical economic (risky) decision stage with known reward magnitudes and probabilities, and foraging decisions with parametric modulation of choice difficulty. The authors report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM8) with cluster-level FWE correction and present cluster coordinates and statistical maps. Contrasts include decision-making condition comparisons (self vs charity) and parametric correlates of task difficulty/foraging value. Participants were healthy university students. Thus the paper meets the fMRI (I4), decision-making contrast (I5), whole-brain group analysis (I6), participant eligibility (I7), and acceptable reporting (I8) inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) are met. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study in human participants using a perceptual decision-making task (random dot motion) with an active control task (arrows). The authors report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (AFNI 3dANOVA3, cluster-corrected maps) and provide cluster tables/coordinates. The key contrast (dots task > arrows control) and ramp-vs-down-ramp interaction test perceptual evidence accumulation (perceptual task > control task and task-related ramping). The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8, and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study in humans where participants performed a risky decision-making task (skewed gambling) during scanning (I4). The paper reports within-task condition contrasts (skewed vs symmetric; positive vs negative skew) suitable as decision-making contrasts (I5). Group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses are described (voxelwise thresholds, cluster correction, second-level regression analyses), satisfying whole-brain evidence requirement (I6). Participants are healthy adults (I7), and whole-brain results are reported in the text/tables/figures (I8). No exclusion criteria are met: contrasts are condition-versus-condition (not task>rest), modality is fMRI (not PET), whole-brain results are provided (not ROI-only), and the task is a risky decision-making paradigm (not excluded task types). Full text appears complete. Therefore the study should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy human participants (n=20) who performed a sequential monetary gambling task involving explicit risky choices (accept vs reject). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (SPM/SnPM) with corrected cluster results and coordinates, and condition contrasts such as accept > reject and parametric modulators (trial outcome, accumulated reward, decision value) that directly compare decision-making conditions (risky vs safe and other within-task contrasts). Full methods, results, and discussion are provided in the text, and whole-brain results are reported in tables/figures. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis (I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) and violates none of the exclusion criteria. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), a canonical risky decision-making task. The paper reports within-task contrasts comparing risky versus riskless decisions (Mean Color > Mean White and Linear Color > Linear White), satisfying the required risky-DM contrast formats. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (FSL FLAME, cluster correction) with coordinates/figures/tables and omnibus and pairwise results, fulfilling the whole-brain evidence requirement. Participant groups (adolescents, including substance users and controls) are acceptable per the eligibility rules. Results are presented in full article sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion) with supplementary figures/tables; the full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not ROI-only, not baseline-only contrasts, not connectivity/resting-state-only, and not non-empirical). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be INCLUDED.

This paper reports an fMRI study in humans performing a modified Iowa Gambling Task (a risky/uncertain decision-making task), and analyzes trial-to-trial prediction-error as a parametric regressor (a within-task contrast). The manuscript includes whole-brain group-level voxelwise analyses (two-sample t tests with cluster correction) and reports within-group one-sample effects of the prediction-error regressor. Thus it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria: I4 (fMRI during a risky decision-making task), I5 (within-task contrast: prediction-error parametric modulation), I6 (group-level whole-brain statistical maps reported), I7 (participant groups acceptable), and I8 (results reported in text/tables/figures). No exclusion criteria appear to apply (not PET, not task>rest only, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and includes within-group task effects). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study reports fMRI data collected while participants performed the Iowa Gambling Task (a risky/ambiguous decision-making task), includes condition contrasts such as risky > safe (choice phase) and other within-task contrasts, presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (ANCOVA, whole-brain and ROI results, with clusterwise maps and coordinates), and includes eligible participant groups (ASD, OCD, and typically developing adolescents). The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets all listed inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study used fMRI while participants performed the Cambridge Gambling Task (meets I4). It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses with cluster tables and figures (meets I6 and I8) and tested healthy human participants (meets I7). However, the paper’s decision-making contrasts reported for the decision stages are predominantly task>rest contrasts (e.g., color decision vs rest; bet decision vs rest). The only reported condition-vs-condition contrast pertains to outcomes (win vs lose) rather than a decision-making contrast of interest (e.g., risky>safe, high-risk>low-risk, ambiguous>non-ambiguous). Therefore it does not provide an admissible decision-making condition-vs-condition contrast as required by I5. Because the study’s decision-related contrasts are only against rest (implicit baseline), it meets exclusion criterion E3. Conclusion: exclude (fails I5; exclusion E3 applies).

This study is excluded because it does not provide the required whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task activation maps (inclusion criterion I6 not met). Although participants performed perceptual decision-making (random-dot motion) inside an MRI scanner (I4 satisfied) and the paper includes condition contrasts relevant to perceptual DM (e.g., low vs. high coherence; I5 satisfied), the manuscript focuses on behavioral analyses and response-time (LBA) modeling and does not report unmasked, whole-brain fMRI task-evoked statistical maps or voxelwise contrasts. No exclusion criteria from the list (E3–E9) explicitly apply. Summary of criteria: inclusion met = I4, I5; inclusion not met = I6 (whole-brain voxelwise maps absent). Therefore EXCLUDED.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (Gabor orientation discrimination) with on-trial subjective certainty ratings. The authors report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts directly comparing decision conditions (correct-unsure vs correct-sure; correct > error), which correspond to high-uncertainty > low-uncertainty / perceptual difficulty contrasts. Whole-brain group analyses (FLAME1) and cluster-corrected maps are reported in text, tables, and figures. Participants are within the eligible population. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not task vs rest-only, and not non-empirical). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria (I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) are satisfied and the study should be INCLUDED.

This paper reports an fMRI experiment with 30 human subjects performing a sequential investment task involving risk (I4). The authors report group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise GLM results: parametric modulation by model-derived TD errors (outcome phase) and Q-values (choice phase), with cluster-corrected whole-brain statistics and reported peak coordinates (satisfies I6 and I8). The analyses constitute task-related contrasts (parametric modulators tested against zero), providing condition/task-related whole-brain contrasts relevant to risky decision-making (I5). Participants are healthy adults (I7). No exclusion criteria are met: this is not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-groups-only, and not a non-empirical paper. Full text appears complete with methods, results (behavioral and fMRI), and discussion (fulltext_incomplete=false). Given these points, the study meets all required inclusion criteria for a meta-analysis of fMRI studies of risky decision-making and should be included.

The study meets several inclusion criteria for the review (it used fMRI during a decision-making reward/number-guessing task [I4]; it reports decision-making versus active control contrasts (Win-Control, Loss-Control) [I5]; the participant sample (youth including clinical and healthy groups) is acceptable [I7]; results/coordinates and ROI results are clearly reported in the text and figures [I8]). However, the group-level statistical testing was conducted and reported within a predefined reward-circuitry ROI (reward circuitry mask) rather than as an unmasked, whole-brain voxelwise task activation map. The manuscript thresholds Z-statistic images within the ROI mask (small-volume/restricted search), and no unmasked whole-brain, voxelwise task activation maps are reported. This violates the requirement for whole-brain evidence (I6) and therefore falls under exclusion criterion E6 (studies reporting only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I4, I5, I7, I8. Inclusion criteria not met: I6. Exclusion criteria applied: E6. Full text appears complete for screening (fulltext_incomplete=false).

This fMRI study tests decision-making processes (probabilistic and risk mechanisms) during pronoun reference resolution, directly manipulating uncertainty and risk. It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM5 second-level random-effects) with condition-vs-condition contrasts (e.g., Undetermined > Directly Determined; Indirectly Determined > Directly Determined) and a parametric uncertainty analysis (high > low uncertainty). Participants are healthy adults. Results are reported with whole-brain coordinates and corrected thresholds. Thus it meets the meta-analysis requirements for fMRI of risky/ambiguous decision-making, includes appropriate contrasts, provides whole-brain group maps, and involves an eligible participant group. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). No exclusion criteria (e.g., task>rest-only contrasts, PET, ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical) are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study of approach–avoidance decisions under probabilistic threat (risky decision-making) that reports condition-wise contrasts across CS threat levels and provides coordinates/tables of activations. It thus satisfies inclusion criteria I4 (fMRI during risky/uncertain decision task), I5 (within-task condition comparisons using contrasts across threat levels/quadratic effects and baseline trials) and I8 (results reported in figures/tables). However, the second-level fMRI analyses were restricted to an a priori ROI mask with small-volume correction rather than a whole-brain, voxelwise group analysis. The paper does not report unmasked whole-brain task-evoked maps, so it fails I6 and meets exclusion criterion E6 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Therefore it must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the perceptual decision-making meta-analysis. It used fMRI while human participants performed multiple perceptual decision-making tasks (face–house, happy–angry face, audiovisual synchrony/asynchrony, and random-dot-motion), satisfying I4. The paper reports condition-vs-condition contrasts that map directly onto perceptual-DM comparisons (e.g., difficult > easy; low coherence > high coherence; asynchrony vs synchrony; noisy > clear), satisfying I5. Analyses were performed at the group level using SPM with whole-brain, random-effects second-level maps and corrected thresholds; activations are reported in tables/figures, satisfying I6 and I8. Participants are healthy adults (I7). No exclusion criteria apply: contrasts are condition-vs-condition (not task>rest) so E3 is not met; imaging modality is fMRI (E4 not met); tasks are perceptual DM (E5 not met); whole-brain results are provided (E6 not met); the paper also reports activations beyond connectivity analyses (E7 not met); this is empirical fMRI data (E9 not met). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion, tables). Therefore include.

The study reports task-based fMRI during a risky decision-making task (Balloon Analogue Risk Task), includes condition-vs-control contrasts (mean pump events vs control-balloon events) and parametric modulation contrasts (risk/reward indexed by pump number), and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise results (cluster-corrected whole-brain analyses). Participant groups (methamphetamine users and healthy controls) are acceptable. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, discussion and limitations, so appears complete. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8, and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human adults using a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task (uncertain outcomes across 80/20, 70/30, 60/40 pairs). The authors report group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) analyses with coordinates and cluster-level FWE correction. Crucially, they include parametric contrasts indexing unsigned prediction error (absolute PE) and its overlap with post-error slowing (i.e., brain activity increasing with surprise/uncertainty), which corresponds to a high-uncertainty > low-uncertainty type contrast relevant to ambiguous/risky decision-making. Results are reported as whole-brain maps and coordinates. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. No exclusion criteria apply (no PET, no ROI-only, not task>rest only, and not only between-group contrasts). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (dot-motion coherence), satisfying the review focus. It reports condition-vs-condition contrasts that map onto perceptual-DM contrasts (e.g., low coherence/hard > high coherence/easy; parametric "inverse dependence on coherence" and explicit "low coherence > high coherence" effects). The paper presents voxelwise, group-level whole-brain analyses with coordinate tables and surface maps (Table 3, figures), meeting the whole-brain evidence requirement. Participants are human and healthy; results are reported in text, figures, and coordinate tables. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not baseline-only contrasts). Full article text including Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion is provided, so fulltext is complete. Hence the study should be INCLUDED.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy human participants (N=22 behavioral, N=21 fMRI) that used a two-armed bandit task with uncertain/reversing reward probabilities, i.e., risky/ambiguous decision-making. fMRI was acquired during task performance and group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (parametric contrasts of decision entropy, relative beliefs/utilities, quadratic and linear regressors). The paper reports within-task condition contrasts and parametric modulations (equivalent to hard>easy / high uncertainty>low uncertainty) with whole-brain corrected maps and coordinates in text/figures/supplement. Participant population is acceptable. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion and fMRI analysis details. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7 and I8; no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

The study reports group-level fMRI during decision-making tasks that involve risk (probabilistic reward task and risky decision task), satisfying the requirement for fMRI during risky decision-making. Neural analyses include parametric task-related contrasts (ventral striatal BOLD correlated with expected value and reward prediction error during choice and outcome periods), which constitute within-task condition contrasts relevant to risky-DM. The methods describe whole-brain acquisition and SPM8 voxelwise analysis and display whole-brain images (reported at uncorrected P<.001), indicating group-level, whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps were produced. Participant groups (depressed and controls) are acceptable per criteria. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not baseline-only contrasts, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not non-empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Hence the study meets inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis of fMRI risky decision-making.

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy human participants manipulating uncertainty via probabilistic (externally attributed) and knowledge-based (internally attributed) decision tasks. It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (random-effects) with thresholding and provides coordinates/tables and figures. Relevant contrasts include experimental conditions versus an active control task (control blocks with arrows) and parametric contrasts of increasing uncertainty (high uncertainty > low uncertainty), satisfying the meta-analysis contrast requirements. The methods, results, and discussion are present in full. Therefore all inclusion criteria (I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports task-based fMRI during a risky decision-making paradigm (Risky Gains Task) in human participants and includes within-task contrasts (risky vs safe decisions; risky wins vs losses). Analyses are whole-brain, voxelwise group-level results (AFNI preprocessing, voxelwise thresholds, cluster correction via updated 3dFWHMx/3dClustSim) with tables/figures reporting significant clusters and coordinates. Participant sample (occasional stimulant users) is acceptable per the review’s participant inclusivity. The paper provides full Methods, Results and Discussion sections and clearly describes the relevant contrasts, satisfying inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) are met: contrasts are condition-vs-condition not task>rest, modality is fMRI not PET, the task is a risky-DM task (not excluded task types), whole-brain results are reported (not ROI-only), and the study reports task activation maps rather than only connectivity or resting-state findings. Thus the study should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (face vs house discrimination with parametrically varied noise). The paper reports within-task contrasts comparing easier (suprathreshold) vs harder (perithreshold) perceptual decisions (e.g., easier > harder), and uses group-level, whole-brain voxelwise GLM analyses with thresholded Z-statistic maps. Results and coordinates are reported in main text and supplementary materials. The full article includes introduction, methods, results and discussion (full text appears complete). Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in human participants (n=18) performing a risky decision-making task manipulating risk pressure. It includes condition-vs-condition contrasts (e.g., riskier > safer, choice_riskier − choice_safer, V_riskier − V_safer, high vs low risk bonus) rather than task>rest, and describes whole-brain, group-level voxelwise GLM analyses with reported peak coordinates and whole-brain effects. Participants are healthy adults. Whole-brain results are reported in the text/figures and methods detail the GLM and group analyses. No exclusion criteria (PET, ROI-only, task>rest-only contrasts, connectivity-only, non-empirical) are met. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a risky financial decision-making task (lottery vs sure win) with whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses. The paper reports condition-versus-condition contrasts (MESSAGE vs NO MESSAGE; ignore vs follow expert) and parametric whole-brain correlations with probability-weighted lottery value and sure-win magnitude, satisfying the requirement for decision-making contrasts. Whole-brain random-effects t-tests and thresholded statistical maps/activation coordinates are reported. The task involves risk (explicit probabilities), not rest-baseline-only contrasts, and is not PET, ROI-only, connectivity-only, nor non-empirical. The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria are met (I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) and no exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study examines social approach/avoid judgment of facial expressions (social decision-making about ambiguous stimuli). Although it meets multiple inclusion criteria for the review (I4: fMRI during an ambiguous decision-making task; I5: contains a decision-making task versus an active control task contrast — social judgment > sex discrimination; I6: reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses; I7: uses an eligible participant group [healthy adults]; I8: whole-brain results are reported in text/figures), it must be excluded because it violates exclusion criterion E5. The task is explicitly social decision-making (approach/avoid), which the review’s exclusion criteria list as not qualifying (e.g., moral or social decision-making is excluded). No other exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical fMRI study of risky decision-making using a two-choice gambling task (Cake Gambling Task) with human participants. The paper reports within-task condition contrasts (High-Risk > Low-Risk; Gain > No-Gain) and parametric contrasts across reward magnitudes. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are described (SPM5; voxelwise t-tests and ANOVAs reported with MNI coordinates and cluster thresholds), and coordinates/clusters are provided in supplementary tables. Participants are healthy human subjects across a wide age range. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis are satisfied and no exclusion criteria are met.

This study reports task-based fMRI in human participants performing a risky decision-making task (choices between sure amounts and gambles with varying probabilities/magnitudes). It includes within-task contrasts addressing risk levels (high-risk vs low-risk loss conditions) and feedback effects, and reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses with familywise-error correction (i.e., whole-brain statistical maps). Participant groups (binge drinkers and healthy volunteers) are acceptable. Whole-brain results are described in text and figures. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET; not ROI-only; contains within-task condition contrasts rather than only task>baseline; reports whole-brain activation maps). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and is INCLUDED.

The study reports an fMRI experiment (BART) administered during scanning (risky decision-making), satisfying I4. It includes explicit condition-vs-control contrasts (Active Pumpsparametric vs Control Pumpsparametric; Active vs Control), satisfying I5. Analyses are whole-brain GLM with voxelwise thresholding and cluster correction and report coordinates and group-level results, satisfying I6 and I8. Participants are healthy adult males (eligible under I7). No exclusion criteria are met: it is not PET (E4), not ROI-only (E6), not connectivity-only (E7) and contrasts are condition-vs-control rather than task>rest (not E3). Full text provided includes introduction, methods, results, discussion and references, so fulltext_incomplete=false. Overall, all required inclusion criteria (I4,I5,I6,I7,I8) are met and no exclusion criteria apply, so the study should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

The study is excluded because its decision-making task is value-based (evaluating and choosing giftcards) but not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making paradigm as required. (a) Exclusion criterion met: E5 (task is not risky, ambiguous, or perceptual DM). (b) Inclusion criteria satisfied: I5 (contains decision > nondecision contrasts / within-task decision vs active valuation trials), I6 (group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses reported), I7 (healthy human participants), I8 (whole-brain results clearly reported in text/figures). (c) Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (does not involve risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). Full text appears complete. Therefore the paper does not meet the central thematic inclusion criterion for this meta-analysis and is excluded.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy humans that collected task-based functional MRI during risky decision-making (choices between options with probabilistic outcomes). The paper reports within-task, between-condition contrasts (affect-rich > affect-poor; affect-poor > affect-rich; region-by-condition interactions) and model-based parametric analyses correlating decision weights with BOLD. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses were performed and described (registration to MNI space, FEAT FLAME 2, cluster correction), with peak coordinates and cluster results reported. Participant sample is within acceptable groups. Results are reported in text, figures, and coordinate tables. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not task>baseline only). Therefore the study satisfies all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis and should be included.

This paper reports an event-related fMRI study in human adolescents performing a risky decision-making task (Colorado Balloon Game) with explicit contrasts between risky decision trials (DecBa) and an active control/baseline directed trial (DirBa) for decision, win, and loss periods. The analyses are whole-brain, group-level random-effects voxelwise maps (SPM) reported with cluster- and voxel-level corrections and coordinates. Participants include clinical (ASD) and control groups (adolescents), which are acceptable. The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion, so the full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not ROI-only, not rest-baseline-only contrasts, not connectivity-only, and not non-empirical). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis of fMRI risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in healthy human participants performing a probabilistic instrumental learning task with binary choices between cues associated with different reward probabilities (25% vs 75%), which constitutes risky decision-making. The authors provide group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) statistical parametric maps for task-related effects: parametric modulators of state value and of left/right option values at cue onset, and prediction errors at outcome. These parametric contrasts constitute within-task decision-related contrasts (i.e., neural correlates of value/risk across conditions) suitable for inclusion. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (not merely abstract/metadata). No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, rest-baseline-only contrasts, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and is eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis of fMRI studies of risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis: I4 — BOLD-fMRI was acquired while human participants performed the Iowa Gambling Task (an ambiguous decision-making task); I5 — the primary contrast is decision-making > active non-gambling control condition (decision-making - control); I6 — group-level, whole-brain voxelwise activation maps are reported (normalization, cluster thresholds, group maps described); I7 — participant groups (newly diagnosed T2DM patients and healthy controls) are acceptable per criteria; I8 — whole-brain results are reported in the text, figures and table descriptions. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not task>rest-only, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and within-group task effects are reported). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and data availability).

This is an fMRI study of risky decision-making using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) with whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses. The GLM includes condition contrasts (active pumps vs control pumps, parametric modulation by pump number, and pumps following cash-out vs explosion), and results are reported as whole-brain maps and region lists. Core article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Thus it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for fMRI risky decision-making and provides the necessary whole-brain contrasts and reporting.

This full-text reports an fMRI experiment in human participants performing risky decision-making (and intertemporal) tasks, with explicit within-task and between-condition contrasts (e.g., Risk > Control, Risk > Delay, Delay > Control, Delay > Risk, and choice-predictive contrasts). Analyses are group-level, whole-brain voxelwise (FLAME, thresholding reported) with coordinates and tables/figures provided. Participant sample (N=23 healthy adults) is within eligible populations. Whole-brain results are clearly described in text, tables, and figures. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not task>rest only). Therefore the study qualifies for inclusion for the meta-analysis of fMRI studies of risky decision-making. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study is excluded because its task is social decision-making (emotion recognition of morphed faces), which falls under exclusion criterion E5 (social decision-making is a non-qualifying task per E5). Despite exclusion, the paper does meet several inclusion criteria: I4 (fMRI was conducted while participants performed an ambiguous decision-making task involving uncertain/ambiguous facial expressions), I5 (it reports within-task contrasts comparing decision events: last face > previous faces), I6 (group-level, whole-brain task-evoked analyses are reported, with FWE-corrected results), I7 (healthy human participants), and I8 (whole-brain results clearly described in text/tables/figures). Inclusion criteria not met: []. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study must be excluded solely because it violates E5 (task domain: social decision-making), even though it otherwise provides appropriate fMRI whole-brain contrasts and analyses.

This is an empirical fMRI study in human participants performing risky and perceptual decision-making tasks (meets I4). It reports a within-task, between-condition contrast (3-phase > 2-phase risk conditions) comparing decision-making conditions (meets I5).
